extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, EPO examiners, and patent practitioners concerned with inventive-step analysis under the EPC
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed refinement of the 'problem and solution' approach to inventive step under Article 56 EPC, focused on how to treat non-technical features when formulating the technical problem. Intended to advise how to apply/comport the Comvik jurisprudence with Articles 54(2) and 56 EPC and to avoid hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem must be known or obvious (state-of-the-art requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formulation of the problem in the problem-and-solution approach is only correct if the problem is known or obvious in view of everything made available to the public before the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from Article 56 EPC (inventive step judged 'having regard to the state of the art') together with Article 54(2) EPC (state of the art = everything made available to the public). If the problem is not obvious in view of the prior art, the problem-and-solution analysis cannot validly establish lack of inventive step. Anti-pattern: formulating a problem that includes novel matter not in the prior art and then using it to show the claimed solution is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-technical features cannot contribute to inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that are wholly non-technical and do not combine with technical features to produce a technical effect cannot be regarded as part of the invention and therefore cannot contribute to inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale based on Article 52(1) EPC: patents are for inventions 'in all fields of technology.' This is the established Comvik 'first rule'—non-technical features are excluded from the inventive-step assessment unless they contribute to a technical effect. Example: decisions consistently treating purely non-technical aspects as irrelevant to inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-technical features may be included in the problem only if known or obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel non-technical features should not be incorporated into the statement of the problem unless their inclusion is known or would have been obvious from what was made available to the public before the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the proposed modification of the Comvik 'second rule': the mere presence of a non-technical aim in a claim does not justify adding it to the problem unless it is part of the prior art. Legal consequence: findings of obviousness cannot be based on features not in the state of the art. Examples/contrast: decision T 2063/09 (BlackBerry) where a non-technical data-limit feature was added to the problem; guidelines' earlier comment that 'requirements specification is not prior art' is inconsistent with Article 56 and has been removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem formulation must avoid pointers to the solution (no hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem should not contain matters of which the skilled person would only have become aware by knowledge of the claimed solution; it must not include pointers to or partially anticipate the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle prevents hindsight and is fundamental to ensuring inventive step is judged against the prior art alone. Comvik part 7 expresses this as a general rule, but the article argues that it must apply to all aspects of the problem (technical and non-technical) unless those aspects are themselves in the prior art. Anti-pattern: including elements in the problem that derive solely from the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate (and treat independently) the two strands of Comvik reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion of non-technical features from contributing to inventive step (removal from the solution) should be distinguished from any rule that permits transferring non-technical features into the problem formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically Comvik conflated these two ideas; the article argues they are independent and should be applied separately: (i) do not let non-technical features supply inventive step (they're ignored in the solution), and (ii) only include non-technical features in the problem if they are known/obvious. This avoids using the problem formulation as a backdoor to penalise claims with novel non-technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem need not be purely technical (but must be known/obvious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Later case law (e.g., T 1784/06 Comptel) indicates that the problem and solution approach does not require the problem to be technical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the problem is non-technical in nature, it may be used in the method so long as the problem itself is part of the prior art (known or obvious). The non-technical character of the problem does not permit inclusion of novel non-technical matter in the problem-formulation step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability should depend only on technical features, not on recited non-technical aims or inventor's motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentability of technical features should not be affected by why the inventor made the invention or by which non-technical aims are recited in particular claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including novel non-technical aims in the problem makes patentability depend arbitrarily on claim drafting or inventor motivation (the same technical features could be patentable or not depending on which non-technical aim is claimed). The refined approach prevents this anomaly by requiring non-technical aims to be prior art before they can be used in the problem formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined Comvik approach for practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim includes non-technical features, assess inventive step by: (a) considering only those features that contribute to a technical effect as part of the invention/solution; and (b) including non-technical features in the problem only if they were known or would have been obvious from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reconciles Articles 52, 54(2) and 56 with Comvik practice: (i) technical features (or combinations producing a technical effect) supply inventive step; (ii) non-technical features may be part of the problem only if in prior art. Example: T 1784/06 supports (i); T 0641/00 Comvik historically supported (ii) in a problematic way; the article cites T 2063/09 as a case where the modified approach would alter the reasoning. Practical effect: examiners/boards should show that any non-technical constraint included in the problem was known/obvious in the prior art rather than inferred from the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the state-of-the-art requirement as an objective test to detect impermissible problem formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that any feature (technical or non-technical) used to formulate the problem can be shown to be part of the prior art; this provides an objective way to spot and prevent impermissible pointers to the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the 'known/obvious in the prior art' test helps avoid hindsight and resolves disputes over problem formulation. It also aligns the problem-and-solution approach strictly with the statutory text of Articles 54(2) and 56 EPC. Anti-pattern: letting the presence of a feature in the claim alone be the justification for its inclusion in the problem.
